## READ

The strongest signal is that management put hard numbers on rising rates: about $500 million of extra wealth NII this year, back-half weighted, plus $200 million from reversing fee waivers, with a further $1.3 billion for each additional 100bp, "largely" falling to the bottom line. That shifts the earnings mix toward more durable revenue while the most volatile piece is already weakening: Q4 fixed income fell 31% and transactional wealth revenue fell 23%. The wealth engine looks structural rather than cyclical. Net new assets were $438 billion (11% growth), with $127 billion in Q4 alone, and Gorman laid out a 5–7% floor rather than a return to the old 3–4%. Management backed that confidence by raising the ROTCE target to 20%+ and the wealth margin target to 30%+, while holding 280bp of excess CET1 that absorbed the SA-CCR adoption. What tempers conviction is that the institutional outlook explicitly "depends on monetary and fiscal policy and its impact on sentiment," and nobody tied the tech-heavy banking book to a number when asked directly.

## SCORE

**+2.** I'd be wrong if the capital-markets slowdown visible in Q4 fixed income spreads into banking and equities faster than rate-driven NII and wealth fees can offset it.

The key point is that Diodes built up distributor inventory while demand was weakening. Management said channel inventory is now above its normal 11–14 week range. Asked about it twice, they never gave the actual number, only saying they are "OK" with it ahead of a China recovery they "anticipate" around Q2. Meanwhile, Q1 guidance of $467M is another roughly 6% sequential drop after Q4's 4.8% decline. Management also expects non-GAAP operating expenses to rise to 22.2% of revenue from 21.3%, which by my math implies non-GAAP EPS near $1.49, down from $1.73 in Q4 and $2.00 in Q3. The real strengths are gross margin held near 41%, record automotive at 17% of product revenue, and auto plus industrial at 45%. But industrial was called "mixed" with inventory rebalancing, and Q4 GAAP EPS of $2.00 was inflated by a 1.5% tax rate. The record full-year numbers look backward; the forward signals point to falling earnings and inventory that could unwind.

## SCORE

**-2.** I'd be wrong if the China and consumer recovery arrives on schedule in Q2, drawing channel inventory back into range and turning revenue up while gross margin holds at about 41%.

The most important signal is that organic growth is accelerating. Excluding the roughly 3.5 points from Kyndryl, revenue grew 5%, the first clean evidence of the mid-single-digit model, and consulting's 16% growth with a 1.2 book-to-bill supports guidance for double-digit consulting growth in the first half. This is tempered by two soft spots in management's answers:

- **Cash flow guidance fell short of the framework.** Free cash flow guidance of $10–10.5B is below the roughly $11.5B one analyst derived from management's own framework. Jim Cavanaugh's bridge (structural charges, working capital, minimal tax help) explained the gap rather than closing it.
- **Earnings questions went unanswered.** When asked whether the margin math implies net income below free cash flow, he flatly declined to talk about EPS.

The underlying software picture is also thinner than the headline 10%:

- About 5 points of that growth came from Kyndryl.
- Transaction processing growth was entirely Kyndryl.
- Security declined, and Data & AI grew only 3%.

Near-term drags are acknowledged: IBM Z was down 4%, first-quarter mainframe softness is expected, currency is a 3-point headwind in Q1, and profit is weighted 40/60 toward the second half. Net, the organic inflection and consulting momentum slightly outweigh the cash flow shortfall and evasiveness on earnings.

## SCORE

**+1.** I would be wrong if Q1 organic growth (ex-Kyndryl, at constant currency) slips back below 4%, or if consulting margins stall under labor cost pressure, which would confirm the soft free cash flow guide as the real signal.

This quarter looks like a storm-hit trough with a clear rebound ahead, but the refining recovery is only asserted, not shown.

**What supports a rebound:**
- Chemicals guidance is concrete. Management expects Q2 utilization in the mid-90s, up from 79%, and "above mid-cycle EBITDA."
- Refining is coming out of heavy maintenance. Utilization was already in the mid-80s in April, and turnarounds finish within 7 to 10 days.
- Management expects fuel demand to return to 2019 levels in the second half of 2021, while more than 1 million barrels per day of U.S. refining capacity has closed since 2019.

**What holds me back:**
- Asked whether refining was profitable in April, as a peer's was by March, Bob Herman did not say yes. He pointed to ongoing maintenance and suggested combining refining with marketing.
- Management admitted rising RIN costs are a net negative. RINs are the credits refiners must buy to meet renewable fuel rules, and Phillips 66 only generates about half of what it needs.
- Operating cash flow of $271M did not cover the $394M dividend, and cash fell from $2.5B to $1.4B.
- Debt is $15B with a negative outlook from the rating agencies. Buybacks and dividend increases are effectively on hold until debt falls toward $12B.

The earnings recovery is real enough to favor mild outperformance, but it is too dependent on refining to hold strong conviction.

## SCORE

**+1.** I would be wrong if Q2 refining is still unprofitable, or if RIN costs keep rising and pull the capture rate (the share of benchmark refining margins the company actually earns) below 40% despite higher utilization.

}

The key signal is a change in earnings mix. Base-business organic growth hit 27% in the quarter, and management raised the full-year base outlook from 8% to 12% (+$850M). At the same time, they cut testing revenue by $900M to $4.9B, which leaves only about $1.1B for the second half. That makes COVID testing a smaller, de-risked piece of the story, with upside if Delta lifts demand, while durable demand from pharma/biotech, academic/government (+35%) and analytical instruments (+36% organic) carries growth. Vaccine and therapy revenue also rose $300M to $1.8B, backed by capacity-constrained backlog and orders at the new Carlsbad plasmid site. The September 17 analyst day, with 2022 scenarios, is a near-term catalyst.

The offsets are real:
- The EPS raise was only $0.10.
- The full-year margin guide slipped about 15 basis points to 29.7%, flat with 2020.
- Management declined to quantify margins excluding COVID revenue, which leaves the 2022 profit baseline unclear.
- PPD will pull the company margin lower once it closes.

## SCORE

**+2.** I'd be wrong if the analyst day or Q3 shows base growth fading well below the 12% pace, or a 2022 framework in which the testing roll-off drives EPS lower year over year.

The top line held up well. Comparable sales were 6.4%, or 7.1% excluding gas, with traffic up 3.1%. EPS excluding discrete tax items grew 13.6%. What moved me, though, is erosion in the membership engine that the whole model rests on:

- **Renewal rates are falling.** The US/Canada rate fell another 10 bps to 92.2%, and Millerchip warned it "may still see a slight decline" over the next few quarters.
- **Member growth is slowing.** Paid members grew 5.2%, and management conceded the slowdown when Kelly asked. They sidestepped his point that the exit rate may be below 5.2%.
- **Margins and costs gave no help.** Core gross margin was flat. Healthcare costs grew faster than sales for the first time, which blocked SG&A leverage.
- **The growth plan was trimmed.** FY26 net openings were cut to 28 because of Spain delays.
- **Non-foods are decelerating.** Management admitted the slowdown as it laps gold and gift-card sales, with no forward guidance.

On the positive side, executive membership grew 9.1% and digital comps grew 20.5%. But the incremental news points to steady rather than accelerating results. That leaves little to push outperformance.

## SCORE

**-1**

This is a weak view. Execution is solid, but the membership and margin signals are softening at the edges, and nothing here signals acceleration.

I'd be wrong if renewal rates stabilize quickly and SG&A leverage shows up next quarter, which would show the digital-cohort issue was transitory.

Honeywell beat the high end of its guidance on every metric: 4% organic growth and adjusted EPS of $2.51, up 7%. It then raised the full-year EPS range to $10.20–$10.50, even after absorbing roughly $0.18 of demand contingency and about $500 million of tariff exposure it says it can fully offset. When pressed by Nigel Cole, the CFO said that contingency is purely top-down: "I don't have any data that would suggest that demand is falling out," and April orders stayed strong. That supports a record $36.1 billion backlog, up 8% organically, and $3 billion of buybacks already this year, about 2% of shares. The weak spots are real but contained. Industrial automation was cut to a mid-single-digit decline, and aerospace margins fell 190 basis points. Most growth now comes from about 3 points of price against flat-to-negative volume, which makes the outlook depend on pricing holding.

## SCORE

**+2.** I would be wrong if China and short-cycle demand turns out worse than the contingency covers, forcing a second-half guidance cut or showing that price increases are destroying volume.

What moved me is a heavy, front-loaded buyback set against a slowing outlook. Management plans to repurchase $2 billion of stock in fiscal 2025, with $1 billion in Q1 alone, and says "the current multiple does not accurately reflect Emerson's strong outlook." That is concrete near-term support backed by delivery: FY24 EPS of $5.49 came in at the high end of guidance, and free cash flow of $2.9B beat guidance.

The fundamentals are cooling, though:

- Underlying orders grew only 2% for the year.
- Test and measurement orders were still down 7% in Q4.
- The FY25 sales guide is 3–5%, down from 6%.
- EPS growth slows to roughly 7–10% ($5.85–$6.05) after three years above 20%.
- The discrete recovery that underpins the guide is back-half loaded, and Q1 sales growth is guided at only 2–3%.

The weakest point is the $240/share AspenTech take-private. Management called it "neutral" to FY25 EPS but declined when Steve Tusa and Julian Mitchell asked for the math on synergies or timing, while confirming it will add debt. The planned sale of safety and productivity would also remove about $0.48 of EPS and $0.2B of free cash flow that the guide still includes.

On balance, the buyback and consistent execution slightly outweigh the unquantified deal risk and decelerating growth over two quarters.

## SCORE

**+1.** I would be wrong if Q1 orders stay near 2% with no improvement in discrete or test and measurement, or if AspenTech terms are raised and prove dilutive.

The headline beat hides a business slowing on every forward-looking measure.

- **Large deals fell.** Deals over $100K dropped to 77 from 97 a year ago, about 20% fewer.
- **Guidance came down.** Management cut full-year revenue guidance and guided net retention down to about 108% from 110%, citing customers cutting headcount and seat expansion.
- **The billings beat was borrowed.** The Q3 billings beat came partly from early renewals pulled forward out of Q4. Q4 billings are guided to only about 10% growth.
- **The next two quarters look weak.** Management flagged that the first half of FY24 brings a gross margin dip of a couple hundred basis points, a temporary operating margin headwind, and about 3 points of FX drag, heaviest in the first half. That combines slower reported growth with a pause in margin expansion, which removes the margin-improvement story the stock has leaned on.

Offsets include record 24% operating margins, 3% churn, a raised EPS guide, and a new $150M buyback. These cushion the downside but do not change the direction of the fundamentals over this window.

## SCORE

**-2.** I would be wrong if Q4 revenue and billings come in clearly above guidance and the FY24 outlook shows reported growth holding near 10% with net retention stable around 110%.

The call's most useful signal is that the cycle has bottomed but is not yet rebounding. Revenue was $166M, up 14% sequentially, and cash generation improved:
- Internal inventory fell $27M, and days of inventory dropped from 217 to 165.
- Operating cash flow was +$32M despite an operating loss.
- Non-GAAP gross margin rose to 54.5% from 53%.

The upside that isn't priced into guidance is the lean channel. Distributor inventory is at 53 days against a 70–75 day target, and the Q4 outlook explicitly assumes no restocking. That leaves room for a positive surprise if demand firms.

The cautions are real, though:
- Q4 guidance is flat at $161–171M, and the company is still loss-making on a non-GAAP basis.
- Industrial is getting weaker, not better. Management said it would "like to see more strength from industrial than we're now seeing."
- Bookings have improved but "not significantly accelerated."
- Management declined to size the 2025 design-win contribution when asked directly. So the "solid growth year" claim, which rests on the CGM and Wi-Fi 917 ramps, is asserted rather than evidenced.

## SCORE

**+1.** Destocking is largely done, the channel is under-stocked, and new product ramps begin in Q4 and Q1. That argues for a mild edge, but flat guidance and industrial softness cap my conviction. I'd be wrong if Q1 guidance comes in below seasonal norms, showing that design-win ramps can't offset a weak industrial market and a seasonally soft quarter.

Dow just posted the best quarter in its history, but the call suggests this is close to the top. Sales rose 66%, and 53 points of that came from price while volume added only 9. When Frank Mitch noted the first half is already running at the "$12 billion or greater" EBITDA that management once called peak, Fidling said Q3 should be "fairly similar." His case for more upside rested on a $1 billion growth-project slate spread "over the next several years," not on anything near term.

Several items point to flat-to-lower Q3 earnings:
- **Q3 headwinds:** about $210M of added turnaround spending plus $100M of non-recurring licensing income that won't repeat.
- **Sales guidance:** Duffy Fisher pointed out that packaging and plastics sales are guided up only 0–2%, even though exit pricing is about 6% above the Q2 average. Management called this volume conservatism.
- **The peak-margin question:** David Begleiter asked about consultants calling July the peak for integrated polyethylene margins. Fidling pointed to a strong July order book but did not rebut the downturn forecast for later in the year.
- **Buybacks:** despite $1.7B of free cash flow, buybacks stay at about $200M a quarter, only enough to offset dilution, as capital spending rises.

On the positive side, customer backlogs are 45–60 days and inventories are at record lows. Still, for a commodity producer at record margins, a guide to "flat" with no bigger capital return is a mild negative signal against the S&P.

## SCORE

**-2**

I would be wrong if polyethylene pricing kept climbing through Q4 and the October Investor Day raised peak-earnings targets alongside a meaningfully larger buyback.

The core insurance business improved more than a price-driven story alone would explain. General insurance accident-year combined ratio ex-CAT improved 290bp to 89.5%, the 15th straight quarter of improvement. North America commercial improved 580bp, and underwriting income rose six-fold to $446M.

The capital story adds to that. The company bought back $1.4B in Q1, committed to at least $1B more in Q2, and received a new $5B authorization. At the Q1 average price of about $60, those two quarters retire roughly 5% of the 800M shares. Interest costs are also falling by about $290M a year, and management says rising rates add about $500M of investment income per 100bp. In April, new-money yields moved above the yields on assets rolling off.

The main concern is inflation. Management raised its short-tail severity trend view toward 5.5% and admitted the sub-90 combined-ratio target was set before inflation spiked. One analyst also noted that loss-ratio improvement is lagging what the earned rate increases would imply.

Two answers were evasive. Management would not give a run-rate ROE for life and retirement against the 12–14% target, and would not give a timeline for removing stranded corporate costs. Life and retirement pre-tax income fell 23%, and the CoreBridge IPO is still "subject to market conditions."

## SCORE

**+2.** I would be wrong if rising loss-cost trends or a stalled CoreBridge IPO erase the underwriting gains and slow the buyback pace.

Management used this call to reset expectations sharply downward. The main points:

- **Margins:** Gross margin falls from 57.8% this quarter to 51–53% "for the next two to three years."
- **Capital spending:** 2022 capex rises to $25–28B, up from $18–19B, with "potential for further growth." Free cash flow will be under pressure.
- **Revenue:** 2022 revenue of "at least $74B" is essentially flat against this year's $73.5B. The 10–12% growth rate is pushed out four to five years. As Ross Seymour noted, Intel has grown double digits only once in the last decade.
- **Quality of the beat:** 47 of the 61 cents of EPS upside came from a McAfee dividend and a one-time tax benefit. Revenue missed its own guide.
- **Data center:** Cloud revenue fell 20% year-over-year, and full-year data center revenue is guided down on a "more competitive environment." When Stacy Raskin pressed on falling data center prices, management answered "mix" and did not address competition.
- **Leadership:** The CFO's retirement and the delayed investor day remove any near-term catalyst.

A holder now faces two to three years of lower margins and heavy spending, justified mainly by roadmap promises.

## SCORE

**-3.** I would be wrong if Alder Lake and Sapphire Rapids ramp on schedule and win back enough pricing and share that margins track toward the top of the range early, with data center cloud revenue recovering by Q1.

Management's tone shifted clearly toward recovery, and several concrete facts support it. The Q3 guide of $3.15B is up 8% sequentially and above normal seasonality. It implies EPS of $3.10 versus $2.72, with operating margin expanding to 33.7%.

The auto upside does not depend on a better car market. Western Tier 1 customers are ending an eight-quarter inventory drawdown, so NXP "starts to ship to natural end demand." Sequential auto growth is roughly doubling from +3% to mid-single digits.

Kurt said all four tracked signals improved over 90 days, and customer supply escalations "almost doubled." Distributor inventory sits at 9 weeks against an 11-week target. That gap is about $200M of refill the guide explicitly excludes, and management says it could start this quarter.

The main pushback came from Stacy Rasgon. Auto end demand is weak, and car-maker (OEM) pre-announcements have been negative. Revenue is still down 3% year-on-year, and communications infrastructure is down in the high-20s percent. There is also a CEO transition: an analyst called this Kurt's last call.

## SCORE

**+2.** Early-cycle inflection plus an unused channel-refill lever gives a modest positive tilt. I would be wrong if the Tier 1 inventory burn turns out not to be ending. In that case, Q3 auto misses the mid-single-digit sequential rise and the "recovery" proves to be short-cycle noise.

Organic sales grew more than 6% on a genuine three-point volume contribution. The U.S. grew 9% against a 12% base, and global share rose 60 bp, so the top line is not just pricing. What moved me most is the setup for the back half. Management says "the majority of the pricing that we've announced has not yet taken place" and that elasticity on September–October increases ran 20–30% below historical norms. The CFO also did not dispute the analyst's math implying a price-cost surplus in H2, since the $2.8B headwind is largely absorbed in H1 and the cost base starts lapping in Q3/Q4. EPS guidance of 3–6% was held despite a roughly 20-point cost headwind that assumes no easing in commodities. The organic sales guide was raised to 4–5%, and buybacks were raised to $9–10B. Against that, gross margin fell 400 bp, productivity was light (about 80 bp), China was flat, SK-II is soft, and management declined to forecast gross margin beyond "sequential progress."

## SCORE

**+2.** Pricing power, share gains and conservative cost assumptions give a defensive staple a modest edge. The biggest margin pressure is already visible and priced into guidance.

I'd be wrong if the February–April U.S. price increases (Tide, Downy, personal health care) trigger a real volume decline or share loss as they hit shelves.

The key finding is that management raised the monetization guide but not the growth guide. Postpaid ARPA guidance rose to "at least 3.5%" from about 3%, and Sievert said service revenue growth should land "closer to 6% than the prior guidance of around 5%." That is real pricing power on top of a record Q1: 1.3M total postpaid net adds, 495K phones, and ARPA up nearly 4%. Postpaid net add guidance, however, was only held at $5.5–6M.

Several things temper this:
- **Churn will hit Q2.** Sievert confirmed that the legacy-plan price increase changes customer bills in Q2, so the churn effects extend across both quarters. Analysts noted that churn is up industry-wide on price actions.
- **Management declined to discuss Q2 gross adds.** They would not give any intra-quarter color when asked about gross adds so far in Q2.
- **EBITDA growth is set to slow.** Core EBITDA grew 8% in Q1, but full-year guidance is "just over 5% at the midpoint," with Peter flagging that investment spending ramps in "Q2 and the balance of the year."
- **Tariffs are a risk to upgrades.** Management said the customer would bear any tariff costs on handsets, which could slow upgrades.

## SCORE

**+1.** A weak positive: pricing power and a raised revenue outlook are durable, but Q2 is likely to show higher churn and slower EBITDA growth that limit near-term upside.

I would be wrong if Q2 postpaid phone churn rises sharply and phone net adds fall well below last year's pace, showing the price increases cost more customers than management says.

The strongest signal is capital return. AIG guided to up to $6 billion of buybacks in 2024 and $4 billion in 2025, backed by a new $10 billion authorization. It projected 550–600 million shares by year-end 2025, well below the 600–650 million range it expects to reach this year. It also raised the dividend 11%.

The underwriting supports those payouts:
- Comparable underwriting income rose 67%.
- The accident-year combined ratio excluding catastrophes was 88.4%, the 10th straight quarter under 90%.
- Excess casualty pricing rose 16%, and Lexington submissions were up more than 50%.

Two things temper my view:
- **Weak premium growth.** Global commercial grew only 1% excluding divestitures, while management reaffirmed high single-digit growth for the full year. That leaves a large gap to close.
- **Upcoming reserve review.** The North America casualty review, covering 44% of reserves, happens in Q2. This is the same 2016–2019 exposure where the industry is taking charges. Management said it made no adjustments this quarter, but that is not the same as the annual detailed review.

Management also would not add detail on the Corebridge deconsolidation timing beyond "before the end of the second quarter, subject to market conditions." The larger buybacks in Q3 and Q4 depend on that sell-down happening.

## SCORE

**+2.** The buyback pace and improving underwriting margins give a moderate edge over the market. I would be wrong if the Q2 casualty reserve review brings a meaningful charge on 2016–2019 accident years, or if the Corebridge sell-down slips and cuts the buyback pace.

## READ

Management cut full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $10–$11 and organic sales to −7% at the midpoint. The CEO admitted they "underestimated the amount of overstock at our machine builders," which is the second forecasting miss this year. The Q2 beat was flattered by a ~$0.30 bonus-accrual reversal. With backlog now drained, Q3 sales and margins will fall sequentially, leaving the year dependent on high-teens sequential order growth in Q4. The CFO said revenue, not the $100M of cost cuts, is "the single biggest contributor" to that Q4 step-up. Blake declined to call Q4 orders a reliable jumping-off point for FY25, and the CFO is departing mid-reset. Those factors outweigh the offsets: a doubled buyback, a ~3% structural headcount cut with $120M carrying into FY25, and April orders that matched plan.

## SCORE

**−2.** I would be wrong if machine-builder destocking clears on schedule and Q3 orders come in above the mid-single-digit sequential guide, which would make the back-half ramp credible and set up a clean FY25 recovery story.
